claims.claim: A prohibition is recorded as a dated passive naming the authority that imposed it and the reason it stands.
claims.source: Le Guin, Rocannon's World (1966), second handbook entry, quoted by Books & Boots
claims.quote: the planet was placed under Interdict by the Allworld HILF Authority
claims.page: second quotation, Control and Taxation Missions

claims.claim: The blogger contrasts the folk-tale style of the novel's opening story with the more factual style of the rest.
claims.source: Books & Boots (astrofella), review of Rocannon's World, 2019
claims.quote: cast in much more factual, sci fi style

claims.claim: Anand Pandian describes Rocannon's World as opening with the ethnographer's survey of hominoid species on one world.
claims.quote: opening with his survey of “hominoid” species on the world
claims.page: paragraph beginning 'Le Guin's books teem with anthropologists'

claims.claim: Le Guin describes Tolkien's vocabulary as unstriking and everything in it as direct, concrete and simple.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, "From Elfland to Poughkeepsie" (1973)
claims.quote: everything is direct, concrete, and simple

claims.claim: Le Guin says prose rhythms are regular, if at all, only on a very much larger and longer scale than metrical feet.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, "Navigating the Ocean of Story: Session 2, Round 1", Book View Cafe, 2016
claims.quote: only on a very much larger, longer scale

claims.claim: Le Guin says prose rhythms are hard to talk about because we have no vocabulary for them.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, "Navigating the Ocean of Story: Session 2, Round 1", Book View Cafe, 2016
claims.quote: we have no vocabulary for them

claims.claim: Le Guin says that whether composing or rewriting she does not think consciously about the rhythmic factors in a story.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, "Navigating the Ocean of Story: Session 2, Round 1", Book View Cafe, 2016
claims.quote: I don’t think consciously about the rhythmic factors in a story

claims.claim: Le Guin says reading aloud makes you aware of a word or phrase that tangles up the pace and needs to be moved or removed.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, "Navigating the Ocean of Story: Session 2, Round 1", Book View Cafe, 2016
claims.quote: a word or a phrase that tangles up the pace

claims.claim: Le Guin says a hesitation while reading your own prose aloud may reveal a fault in the rhythm.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, "Navigating the Ocean of Story: Session 2, Round 1", Book View Cafe, 2016
claims.quote: Wherever you hesitate in your reading aloud may reveal a fault

claims.claim: Le Guin says her own specimen general description of an invented town, placing Horb on the coast of the southernmost of nine continents, implies very little.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, "Navigating the Ocean of Story: Session 2 — Three New Questions", Book View Cafe, 21 March 2016
claims.quote: This general description implies very little
claims.page: answer to Nicole and Bayla, world-building demonstration

claims.claim: Le Guin says her second specimen sentence about Horb lets the reader learn that the place has a long-established trading economy without stating it.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, "Navigating the Ocean of Story: Session 2 — Three New Questions", Book View Cafe, 21 March 2016
claims.quote: it has a long-established trading economy
claims.page: answer to Nicole and Bayla, world-building demonstration

claims.claim: Le Guin says the difference between her two specimen descriptions is specificity, and prescribes packing sentences with specifics, not with generalities.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, "Navigating the Ocean of Story: Session 2 — Three New Questions", Book View Cafe, 21 March 2016
claims.quote: packing your sentences with specifics, not with generalities

claims.claim: Le Guin says a writer can fake quite a lot or leave it unsaid so long as the invented world looks and smells and tastes real.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, "Navigating the Ocean of Story: Session 2 — Three New Questions", Book View Cafe, 21 March 2016
claims.quote: so long as your world looks and smells and tastes real
claims.page: final answer to Nicole and Bayla

claims.claim: Le Guin says that with an invented world you have to describe more than a realist does.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin interviewed by John Plotz, Public Books, 15 June 2015
claims.quote: you have to describe more than a realist does
claims.page: answer on describing an invented world

claims.claim: Le Guin says she has learned to stop fiddling and twiddling because fiction needs a certain roughness.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, interview excerpts, "A Return to Earthsea", Locus Magazine, September 2001 (Locus Online excerpts page)
